title: Order statistics
objectives: Find the distribution of a minimum, a maximum and the $k$th smallest of independent draws
Judge the best of many tries against the expected maximum

screens.title: The first of five
screens.prose: Five issuers each default at a hazard of 2% a year, independently. One issuer alone has a mean wait of 50 years. Each trial records the time of the **first** default.

state.caption: Five issuers, each with hazard 2% a year. Run the trials.

screens.question: About how long until the first default, on average?

options.why: That is one issuer's mean wait. With five issuers running, someone defaults sooner.
That would be the mean for two issuers. Five clocks are running at once.
Five is too fast: that would need ten issuers. The bars sit nearer 10 years.

hints.text: Run 10,000 trials and look at where the bars balance.
One issuer alone takes 50 years. How does five clocks racing change that?

feedback.correct: About 10 years: the five clocks together run five times as fast as one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the trials and see where the bulk of the bars lies.

byKey.fifty: That is one issuer's mean wait. With five issuers running, someone defaults sooner.
byKey.twentyfive: That would be the mean for two issuers.
byKey.five: Five is too fast: that would need ten issuers.

explain.text: The first default arrives after about 10 years, one fifth of 50. The bars look exponential: the next screen shows why.

screens.title: Everyone must survive
screens.prose: The first default is after $t$ only if all five issuers survive past $t$. Each survives with chance $e^{-0.02t}$, independently.
screens.question: Write $P(\min > t)$ as a function of $t$.

hints.text: Independent survivals multiply.
Five factors of $e^{-0.02t}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the five survival chances.

byKey.one: That is one issuer's survival. All five must survive.
byKey.cdf: That is $P(\min \le t)$. The question asks for survival.
byKey.five: Chances of independent events multiply, not add.

explain.text: $P(\min > t) = \left(e^{-0.02t}\right)^5 = e^{-0.1t}$. This is the survival function of an exponential with rate $0.1$: the first default is exponential, with mean 10 years. The rates $5 \times 0.02$ simply add.

screens.title: Within a year
screens.prose: The first default is exponential with rate 0.1 a year, as the last screen showed.
screens.question: What is the chance the first default comes within one year?

hints.text: Use $P(\min \le t) = 1 - e^{-0.1t}$ with $t = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the exponential CDF with rate 0.1.

byKey.single: 0.0198 is the chance for one issuer. Five issuers raise it.
byKey.five: 0.0990 is five times one issuer's chance. That double counts the years in which two issuers might default.

explain.text: $1 - e^{-0.1} = 0.0952$, a little below $5 \times 0.0198 = 0.0990$. Adding the five chances counts the rare case of two defaults twice.

screens.title: The largest of five
screens.prose: Now take five independent uniforms on $[0, 1]$. The largest is at most 0.9 only if every draw is at most 0.9.
screens.question: What is $P(\max \le 0.9)$?

hints.text: All five draws must be at most 0.9.
Independent chances multiply: five factors of 0.9.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. All five draws must fall below 0.9.

byKey.single: 0.9 is the chance for one draw. All five must pass.
byKey.comp: 0.4095 is $1 - 0.5905$, the chance that the maximum exceeds 0.9.

explain.text: $0.9^5 = 0.5905$. The same trick as the minimum: an event about the extreme is an event about every draw. For the maximum, the CDF is $F(t)^n$.

screens.title: Extremes by their CDFs
screens.prose: You turned an event about the extreme into an event about every draw. For $n$ independent draws with CDF $F$: $P(\max \le t) = F(t)^n$ and $P(\min > t) = (1 - F(t))^n$. Differentiating the first gives $f_{\max}(t) = n\,F(t)^{n-1}f(t)$.
screens.question: For five uniforms on $[0, 1]$, what is the density of the maximum at $t = 0.9$?

hints.text: Here $F(t) = t$ and $f(t) = 1$.

byKey.cdf: 0.5905 is the CDF $0.9^5$, a probability. The density is its slope.
byKey.single: 4.5 is $5 \times 0.9$. The power should be $n - 1 = 4$, not 1.

explain.text: The slope of $t^5$ at 0.9 is $5 \times 0.9^4 = 3.2805$. The density is high near 1: five draws almost always put one of them near the top.

screens.title: The $k$th smallest
screens.prose: Take $n$ independent uniforms on $[0, 1]$ and ask for the density of the $k$th smallest at $x$. Count how a draw can land at $x$, with $k - 1$ below it and $n - k$ above it.
screens.question: Put the counting argument in order.

lines.text: Choose which draw lands in $[x, x + dx]$: $n$ ways, each with chance $dx$
Among the other $n - 1$ draws, choose which $k - 1$ fall below $x$: $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ ways
Each of those $k - 1$ is below $x$ with chance $x$, and each of the $n - k$ others is above with chance $1 - x$
Multiply and divide by $dx$: $f_{(k)}(x) = n\binom{n-1}{k-1}x^{k-1}(1 - x)^{n-k}$

hints.text: First fix the draw that sits at $x$. Then split the others.
The probabilities come after the counts.
Pick the draw, pick those below, attach probabilities, multiply.

feedback.correct: Pick the draw, pick those below, attach probabilities, then multiply.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the arrangements before attaching chances.

byKey.below: The choice of which draws fall below $x$ comes after the draw at $x$ is fixed.
byKey.prob: The chances attach to the arrangement you have just counted.
byKey.mult: The product is the last line, once every factor is known.

explain.text: The $n\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ factor counts arrangements and the powers are the chances. For $k = n$ it reduces to $n x^{n-1}$, the density of the maximum from the last screen.

screens.title: The second smallest of five
screens.prose: Take $n = 5$ and $k = 2$. The second smallest of five uniforms has density $f_{(2)}(x) = 5\binom{4}{1}x(1 - x)^3$.
screens.question: What is the density of the second smallest at $x = 0.3$?

hints.text: The constant is $5 \times 4 = 20$.
Multiply: $20 \times 0.1029$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the constant $5\binom41 = 20$ in front of $x(1 - x)^3$.

byKey.half: 1.029 uses $\binom52 = 10$ in place of $5\binom41 = 20$. The extra factor $n$ counts which draw lands at $x$.

explain.text: $20 \times 0.3 \times 0.7^3 = 2.058$. The mean of the $k$th smallest is $\tfrac{k}{n+1}$, here $\tfrac26$: the draws cut $[0, 1]$ into $n + 1$ gaps of equal mean. This is a Beta density, named in the next lesson.

screens.title: The best of twenty
screens.prose: Twenty strategies with no skill each have a $t$-ratio that is roughly a standard normal. Each trial keeps the **best** one. Run the trials.

state.caption: Each trial draws 20 independent standard normals and keeps the largest.

screens.question: Where does the average best-of-20 $t$-ratio sit?

options.text: At 0, because each draw has mean 0
options.why: Each draw has mean 0, but the best of twenty is the top of a crowd. It is almost never below 1.
A single draw reaches 3 about once in 740. Even with twenty tries it happens only about one trial in 40.

options.text: About 1, one sd above the mean
options.why: That is a typical single good draw. With twenty tries, the best is nearly always above 1.

hints.text: Run 10,000 trials and see where the bulk of the bars lies.
A single draw is above 1 about 16% of the time. With twenty tries, one almost always is.

feedback.correct: The bars centre near 1.9: that is the expected maximum of 20 normals, 1.8675.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the trials and look at the centre of the bars.

byKey.zero: The best of twenty is almost never below 1.
byKey.three: Three-sigma draws are rare even with twenty tries.
byKey.one: With twenty tries, the best is nearly always above 1.

explain.text: The mean of the best of 20 standard normals is $1.8675$ (integrating $z \cdot 20\,\varphi(z)\,\Phi(z)^{19}$). The bars centre near it. Luck alone produces an impressive-looking best strategy.

screens.title: First default within ten years
screens.prose: One issuer alone defaults within 10 years with chance $F(10) = 1 - e^{-0.2} = 0.1813$. Five issuers are independent, each at hazard 2%.
screens.question: What is the chance that at least one of the five defaults within 10 years?

hints.text: "At least one" is the opposite of "none".
None default within 10 years with chance $(1 - 0.1813)^5 = e^{-1}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance that none default, then subtract it from 1.

byKey.maxcdf: 0.0002 is $0.1813^5$: the chance that all five default within 10 years. That is the maximum's CDF, not the minimum's.
byKey.five: 0.9063 is $5 \times 0.1813$. Adding overcounts the cases where several issuers default.

explain.text: $P(\min \le t) = 1 - (1 - F(t))^n$, not $F(t)^n$ (that is $P(\max \le t)$) and not $nF(t)$ (that overcounts overlaps). With $t = 10$ it is $1 - e^{-1}$.

screens.title: First default by simulation
screens.prose: Check the formula by brute force. Each trial draws one default time per name and keeps the earliest. The exact answer is $1 - e^{-(\lambda_1 + \dots + \lambda_n)T}$.
screens.question: Write `first_default_mc(rates, years, trials, seed)`.

widget.starter:
import random


def first_default_mc(rates, years, trials, seed):
    # share of trials in which at least one name defaults within `years`.
    # rng.expovariate(rate) draws one default time.
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    ...
widget.how: Submit runs 6 hidden tests. Three compare the share with $1 - e^{-\sum\lambda T}$ within a stated tolerance, and three check the extreme cases (a zero horizon, huge rates, a share at most 1).

hints.text: In each trial, draw `rng.expovariate(r)` for every rate and take the minimum.
Count the trials whose minimum is at most `years`.
`hits += 1` when `min(...) <= years`, then return `hits / trials`.

feedback.correct: The simulated share matches $1 - e^{-\sum\lambda T}$ in every case.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count a trial when the earliest of the draws is within `years`.

explain.text: The simulated shares match $1 - e^{-\sum\lambda T}$ to within sampling error, which shrinks like $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{\text{trials}}}$. The formula replaces 200,000 random draws with one line.

screens.title: Ties are possible for dice
screens.prose: For continuous variables a tie has probability 0, so $\max$ and $\min$ are never shared. For whole-number variables a tie is possible. The grid shows the larger of two dice.
screens.question: What is $P(\max = 3)$ for two fair dice?

hints.text: Count the cells of the grid in which the larger die is exactly 3.
Subtract: $P(\max \le 3) - P(\max \le 2)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The maximum equals 3 when the larger die is 3, with either die the larger.

byKey.both: $\tfrac{1}{36}$ is the chance that both dice show 3. The maximum is also 3 when one die is 3 and the other is lower.
byKey.cdf: 0.25 is $P(\max \le 3) = \left(\tfrac12\right)^2$. That includes totals of 1 and 2 as well.

explain.text: $P(\max = 3) = F(3)^2 - F(2)^2 = \tfrac{9}{36} - \tfrac{4}{36} = \tfrac{5}{36}$. For discrete variables you subtract two CDF values, because the CDF jumps. For continuous variables a point has no chance, so only the CDF and density matter.

screens.title: The best of twenty backtests
screens.prose: A team tests 20 skill-free strategies, each with a $t$-ratio that is roughly $N(0, 1)$, independent of the others. They report the best, with $t = 2.1$, as significant.
screens.question: What is the chance that the best of the 20 skill-free strategies reaches $t \ge 2.1$?

hints.text: The best misses 2.1 only if every strategy does.
One strategy stays below 2.1 with chance $\Phi(2.1) = 0.9821$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance that all 20 stay below 2.1, then subtract from 1.

byKey.single: 0.0179 is the chance for one strategy. The team has 20 tries.
byKey.times: 0.3573 is $20 \times 0.0179$. It overcounts the cases where two or more strategies clear 2.1.

explain.text: Luck alone gives a $t \ge 2.1$ about 30% of the time, and the best of 20 averages 1.87. A fair benchmark for a chosen-best strategy is the distribution of the maximum, not 0. This is why the backtest lessons stress the number of tries.

ideas: An event about the minimum or maximum is an event about every draw: $P(\max \le t) = F(t)^n$ and $P(\min > t) = (1 - F(t))^n$.
The first default among independent exponentials is exponential with the rates added. The $k$th smallest of $n$ uniforms has density $n\binom{n-1}{k-1}x^{k-1}(1 - x)^{n-k}$ and mean $\tfrac{k}{n+1}$.
The best of many tries is far above a typical draw: the expected maximum of 20 standard normals is 1.87.

formula.name: Order statistics
formula.tex: F_{\max}(t) = F(t)^n, \qquad F_{\min}(t) = 1 - (1 - F(t))^n, \qquad f_{(k)}(x) = n\binom{n-1}{k-1}x^{k-1}(1 - x)^{n-k}
formula.note: For continuous variables ties have chance 0. For discrete ones subtract two CDF values.

summary.trap: $F(t)^n$ is the maximum's CDF, not the minimum's. Adding $nF(t)$ overcounts overlaps.

quiz.prose: Three independent exponential waits have rates 1, 2 and 3 a year.
quiz.question: What is the chance that the shortest of them exceeds half a year?

feedback.correct: The minimum is exponential with rate 6, so $e^{-3} = 0.0498$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the three rates to get the rate of the minimum.

byKey.one: 0.6065 is the chance that the rate-1 wait alone exceeds half a year. All three must.
byKey.time: 0.0025 is $e^{-6}$: the rate 6 is right but $t = 0.5$ is missing from the exponent.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. All four draws must be at most 0.5.

byKey.half: 0.5 is the chance for one draw. All four must be at most 0.5.
byKey.quarter: 0.25 is $0.5^2$. There are four draws, so four factors.

explain.text: Four independent draws, each at most 0.5 with chance 0.5: $0.5^4 = 0.0625$.

quiz.prose: Nine independent uniforms on $[0, 1]$ are sorted.
quiz.question: What is the mean of the third smallest?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The mean of the $k$th smallest of $n$ is $\tfrac{k}{n+1}$.

byKey.kn: $\tfrac39$ divides by $n$. Nine draws split $[0, 1]$ into ten gaps, so divide by $n + 1 = 10$.

explain.text: Nine points cut $[0, 1]$ into ten equal-mean gaps. The third point sits 3 gaps in: $\tfrac{3}{10}$.

quiz.question: What is the chance that the best of them is below 1.5?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. All 20 must stay below 1.5.

byKey.single: 0.9332 is the chance for one. All 20 must stay below 1.5.
byKey.comp: 0.7491 is the chance that the best clears 1.5. The question asks for the best being below.

explain.text: $\Phi(1.5) = 0.9332$ and $0.9332^{20} = 0.2509$. Three times in four, the best of 20 skill-free strategies reaches at least 1.5.
